If he smiles at his phone, if he’s five minutes late, my mind just locks on it and runs through every possible scenario.

At work I’m fine when I’m focused on prescriptions and protocols, but the moment things quiet down, it’s like this loop starts: images of him with someone else, questions about what he might be doing. I know it sounds irrational, and part of me can see that I might be reading too much into tiny details, but the scenes in my head feel very vivid and keep replaying.

I do check his social media sometimes and reread old messages, but I’m not sure if that’s just normal worry or something else. It’s starting to affect my sleep and how relaxed I feel at home.
D004-D016_h024.question_a:

I know everyone says I’m overreacting, but I see “signs” everywhere—how he checks his phone, if he’s five minutes late, a random perfume smell at the pharmacy that I’m sure is on his clothes later. It feels like my brain just locks onto these things and spins them into a narrative that he’s hiding someone from me.  

I get these thoughts stuck in my head, like intrusive images of him with another woman, and they loop over and over. It feels less like a worry and more like a certainty I can’t shake. I’ll replay his text tone in my mind or the way he said something and convince myself it proves he’s lying.  

At work I can still focus, fill prescriptions, counsel patients; no one’s complained. I don’t do any rituals or checking over and over again—no rereading messages or stalking him online. I just sit there stewing in this belief, getting more and more upset, even though I can’t point to anything concrete.

It doesn’t feel like a normal worry; it’s more like an image or thought that just slams into my head while I’m counseling a patient or counting pills. I’ll picture him with someone else, and my chest tightens. Then I feel compelled to “check” things to calm down. I go through his phone over and over, reread old texts between us, recheck his location history, and ask him the same questions repeatedly—sometimes several times in one evening—until I feel a tiny bit of relief.

That relief never lasts. Within minutes my mind starts again: “What if you missed something? What if he’s lying?” I know it doesn’t make sense, and I’m embarrassed by it, but resisting the checking makes me unbearably anxious.

At first it was just this passing idea that I could pick up on things other people couldn’t—like knowing which patients were going to crash before their vitals changed. I told myself it was just experience, but it feels more than that, like I have some kind of special gift or role and people just haven’t realized it yet.

At the same time, I get these thoughts that pop into my head over and over, and I can’t shut them off. Sometimes it’s about me being chosen for something important, sometimes it’s darker—like if I make the wrong decision with a patient, something terrible will happen because the “universe” is watching me. I know it sounds odd, and part of me knows it might not be true, but the thoughts keep coming back. I find myself going over the same ideas in my head, replaying shifts, checking myself, but I’m not sure if that’s just me overthinking or something else.
D004-D016_h025.question_a:
It’s been going on for a little over a year now. I keep having this fixed sense that I’m meant for something huge in medicine, like I’ve been chosen in some way. It’s not just ambition. I honestly feel like I have a special gift to heal people that other nurses and even doctors don’t have. When I’m on the ward, I catch myself thinking the patients do better when I touch them or talk to them, like I’m the real reason they’re improving.

These thoughts pop into my head all the time, almost like they’re intruding on whatever I’m doing. I’ll be charting or giving meds and suddenly I’m thinking, “You’re different, you’re going to change how healthcare works,” and it’s hard to shake. I don’t do any rituals or checking or anything to make the thoughts go away; I just kind of live with them and plan around them, like reading research articles because I feel I need to prepare for this “role.”

Outside of this, I still manage my shifts, pay my bills, hang out with friends. My work performance reviews are fine. It’s mainly this belief and the way it colors how I see my job and my future that’s causing me stress.
D004-D016_h025.question_b:

I keep having these thoughts that if I don’t do certain things perfectly, something terrible will happen to my patients, like I’ll somehow “infect” them with something only I can control. It’s like this voice in my head saying I have some kind of special power over whether people live or die, just by what I touch or how I move. A part of me knows that sounds ridiculous, but in the moment it feels very real and terrifying.

Because of that, I’m constantly washing my hands, not just at work but at home—over and over, for several minutes at a time, until they’re red and cracked. I’ll re-check IV pumps and medication labels repeatedly, sometimes three or four times, even when I know they’re right. If I try to resist the rituals, my anxiety shoots through the roof and the thoughts get louder, like I’m a horrible nurse and something awful will happen because I didn’t “neutralize” it properly. It’s exhausting and it’s starting to affect my shifts and my social life.
